findings.text: The first lines tell a newcomer what Athena is and how it works. The next two paragraphs explain that this page is a sample study and why it exists. A newcomer can quickly say what they are looking at.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The next step is linked from the header and easy to find. But the install step assumes the reader has already cloned the repository, and it names no prerequisites (for example a Rust toolchain or model API keys). A newcomer has to leave the page to learn how to actually start.
findings.source: Heading "Next steps": "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: This is Athena's site, yet almost everything below the header is detail about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets one paragraph on it, plus the evidence of what it can produce.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the whole body from "Start here" to "Claims and sources"

findings.text: The "Start here" section is a good entry point. It has a one-sentence definition, terms defined before use, and an 8-step walk through one task. A reader who stops there still comes away understanding firstmate.
findings.source: Heading "Start here": "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."

findings.text: "Pin" means two different things on this page. The glossary defines it as the study's commit, but the t8 card uses it for a secondmate's harness setting. A newcomer who looks it up gets the wrong meaning.
findings.source: t8 card: "a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none"; Glossary "pin": "The single firstmate commit the study read"

findings.text: "Open captain call" appears many times (Start here, t9, ra5) but is never defined, and the glossary has no entry for it. "Endpoint" and "wake" (in "stale wake") are also used without definitions.
findings.source: "If the backlog item is still an open captain call, teardown reopens it instead of closing it."

findings.text: Secondmates are introduced only by what they are not. The page never says what a secondmate is for, so the newcomer meets a concept they cannot place.
findings.source: Heading "What firstmate is": "A secondmate is a persistent home, not a backlog item."

findings.text: Some transition cards pack many conditions into one long run-on sentence. These are hard for a first-time reader to follow, unlike the clearer "Start here" lists.
findings.source: t4 card, Guard: "worktree clean and committed work landed, whether the captain approved the merge, firstmate merged it under yolo, or a local-only ship landed by a guarded fast-forward; a local-only project also counts..."

findings.text: The page says plainly that nothing was run, and it states unknowns as unknowns, for example "this page gives no test for it" for "in scope". This helps a newcomer trust the page and judge how far to rely on it.
findings.source: Heading "Limits of this study": "This study read the pinned tree only... so no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: This closing note refers to a folder inside the repository without linking to it. It means nothing to a newcomer.
findings.source: Heading "About this page": "is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
